catalog_quote: [3.6] There is no rigorous phonological difference between clitics, suffixes, and postposed particles such as postpositions. Stress and accent patterns, which in other languages of the world often bring out cliticization, are not relevant to Nanga. ... [2.1] Nanga has a typical Dogon stem-level tonal system, with at least one (lexical) high tone element per stem. At the level of syllables, tones are H[igh], L[ow], <HL> (falling), <LH> (rising), and bell-shaped <LHL>. There are no <HLH> syllables. ... Verb stems are lexically /LH/ or /H/. ... Several suffixes impose specific tone overlays on the preceding stem, overriding lexical tones. ... [3.2.2] Segmental phonological rules generally point to a trochaic bias, i.e. bisyllabic [sw] with a strong followed by a weak. tone_statements.citation: Heath, Jeffrey. 2015. Dogon lexical tones of stems. Unpublished comparative/typological manuscript (header: 'last update December 2014'), Dogon and Bangime Linguistics project (dogonlanguages.info), 6 pp.
tone_statements.quote: In eastern Dogon languages, the typical situation is that verbs are either lexically /H/ or /LH/. ... The /LH/ melody on trisyllabics is realized as Cv̀.Cv̀.Cv́ (L.L.H) or as Cv̀.Cv́.Cv́ (L.H.H) depending on the language, as shown in (2). (2) a. L.L.H eastern: Toro Tegu, Jamsay, Ben Tey, Donno So ... b. L.H.H (s.t. varying with L.H.L) eastern: Nanga, Bankan Tey, Togo Kan northwestern: Najamba ... In eastern Dogon languages, typical lexical melodies for uncompounded stems other than verbs are /H/, /HL/, /LH/, and /LHL/. ... Possible examples of /HLH/ in Nanga and Ben Tey might be analysed as compounds. ... Nanga appears to have relexified *Cv́Cv̀ as Cv́Cv̂, with final falling tone.

tone_statements.quote: Based on semantic scope, for example, Nanga sequences of the type Poss-N-Dem should be realized as Poss NL Dem, with the (higher) demonstrative winning the battle to control the tone ovelay on the noun. The actual output, however, is ⊂Poss H(L)N⊃ Dem as in (3). (3) ⊂yǎ-m HLínjɛ̀⊃ mǔ:. ⊂woman-AnPl HLdog⊃ Prox.AnPl or 3SnSg ‘these woman’s dogs’ (=‘these dogs of a woman’)

audit.reasoning: The classification 'tonal, no stress rule' rests on the only existing description of Nanga, a 444-page 2016 reference grammar by the language's sole documenter, which we hold and whose deciding sentences ('Stress and accent patterns.. are not relevant to Nanga'; 'typical Dogon stem-level tonal system'; 'trochaic bias' from segmental rules only) are confirmed verbatim at the cited pages. Glottolog lists no other descriptive work; web search turned up only tonosyntax studies (McPherson 2014 diss., downloaded; McPherson & Heath 2016 NLLT) that reuse Heath's data and are silent on word stress. Nothing better exists and nothing suggests the classification is wrong.

sources.citation: McPherson, Laura E. 2014. Replacive grammatical tone in the Dogon languages. PhD dissertation, University of California, Los Angeles. 370 pp.
sources.quote: Treats Nanga as a lexical+replacive grammatical tone language ('Nanga is one of the most tonosyntactically complex languages in the sample', p. 163); data explicitly from Heath's grammar drafts. No statement on Nanga word stress; the only 'stress' discussion (sec. 2.7.2, p. 118) is a diachronic speculation that Dogon tonal overlays originated in phrasal de-emphasis, not a synchronic stress claim.

sources.note: Eastern Dogon verbs (incl. Nanga) are lexically /H/ or /LH/, melody largely predictable from initial obstruent voicing; Nanga is a 'left-edge tone break' language (trisyllabic /LH/ = L.H.H, sometimes varying with L.H.L), grouped with Bankan Tey and Togo Kan; Nanga 'bring' jě: /LH/ regular; non-verb stems have melodies /H/, /HL/, /LH/, /LHL/ (no lexical /L/, /HLH/ marginal -- possible Nanga /HLH/ items analysable as compounds); Nanga has relexified *Cv́Cv̀ as Cv́Cv̂ with final falling tone; syllable tones H, L, <HL>, <LH>, occasionally <LHL>; grammatical overlays erase lexical melodies.

The actual output, however, is ⊂Poss H(L)N⊃ Dem as in (3). (3) ⊂yǎ-m HLínjɛ̀⊃ mǔ:. ⊂woman-AnPl HLdog⊃ Prox.AnPl or 3SnSg ‘these woman’s dogs’ (=‘these dogs of a woman’)

sources.note: Lays out the Dogon system of lexical melodies vs. floating tonal morphemes vs. syntactically controlled word-level overlays ({L}, {HL}, {H}) imposed by possessors, adjectives, demonstratives, relative clauses; for Nanga specifically: Poss-N-Dem surfaces as an island [Poss HL-N] Dem (possessor-controlled {HL} on the noun survives the higher demonstrative), ex. yǎ-m ínjɛ̀ mǔ: 'these woman's dogs'. Grammatical tone only; no lexical inventory statement for Nanga here.
